item.title: Trump says he knows 'nothing' about his crypto firm. Democrats want answers.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON – President Donald Trump told "60 Minutes" this week he knew “nothing” about the World Liberty Financial crypto company that helped him take in more than $2 billion last year alone. Democrats who’ll take control of Congress in January have big plans to find out more. The incoming heads of various oversight committees are already naming a broad array of investigative targets regarding Trump’s personal and administrative actions. They’re demanding records, promising subpoenas – and warning people and companies not to destroy any documents. "If you are a member of the Trump crime family and you're grifting off the American public, you should lawyer up,” Rep. Robert Garcia, D-California, who is poised to chair the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee in January, told MS NOW's Lawrence O'Donnell two days after the Democrats’ Nov. 3 blowout win in the midterms. In response, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told USA TODAY: “If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people.” This week, White House Counsel Will Scharf warned Garcia that aggressive oversight of the Trump administration and threats against administration officials “may cross the line into blatant criminality,” especially if their investigations are used to “harass and aggrandize” as opposed to advancing legitimate legislative policies. Garcia wasted no time in replying , saying in a statement posted to X: "It appears Donald Trump has something to hide. Let's be clear: Congress' authority comes from Article I of the Constitution, not from the permission of the White House. Congress has wide latitude to conduct investigations and oversight, an authority inherent in the power to legislate.” Garcia told Punchbowl News his committee will look at the Trump family's crypto deals, Donald Trump Jr. 's business dealings and family members , including son-in-law Jared Kushner, who are "sitting on boards and getting contracts." Garcia has also asked the Pentagon's inspector general to investigate whether companies linked to Trump’s two eldest sons won defense contracts. The Trump family's cryptocurrency ventures are likely to be the first target in both the House and Senate, with the president's financial disclosure filing and news reports estimating those ventures brought Trump and his family more than $1.4 billion in 2025. That’s especially the case for World Liberty, which Trump co-founded in September 2024 with his sons and the sons of his Middle East and Russia-Ukraine war envoy, Steve Witkoff. Trump said his sons run it. Democrats want answers, for instance, about how much Trump made off the crypto venture, how much he knew about its business dealings – and how a $500 million deal first reported by The Wall Street Journal went down. More: How much money did Trump make in first 100 days? Crypto deals raise questions The Journal reported in January that an investor linked to the United Arab Emirates government secretly signed a deal to buy a 49% stake in World Liberty just before Trump's inauguration. The UAE has since been seeking favorable treatment from the Trump administration on a number of important issues, including the purchase of advanced AI computer chips. The president’s own sales of a Trump-branded memecoin, international real estate deals involving the Trump Organization and special access to the president for top memecoin investors are also seen as early avenues of investigative inquiry, Democrats said. Trump's pardon of Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao, whose company helped the Trump family launch a stablecoin, has been a target of Garcia and other Democrats long before their sweeping victory in the midterms. What Trump said about his family's finances For years, Democrats in the House and Senate have been publicly accusing Trump and his family of corruptly profiting from business dealings linked to foreign governments. Trump pledged before his first term in office that the Trump Organization would not seek or enter into any new foreign business deals while he was in the White House. He made no such promise this time around. In a Nov. 8 interview on "60 Minutes," Ross Douthat asked whether Trump would call it corrupt if former President Joe Biden was part owner of a company like World Liberty Financial “and it has all of these investments from the Middle East.” "Here's the difference," Trump replied. "I'm gonna tell you why. Because I know nothing about it." More: Congressional Democrats attack Donald Trump's 'corrupt' crypto connections Asked why he didn't simply divest to protect himself from accusations of corruption, Trump said his sons run the family business: “It's hard to say to them, 'Don't do anything anymore for four years because I'm president.’” Douthat pointed to a Forbes estimate that Trump's net worth has grown by $3 billion since retaking the White House. "I devote almost no time to my net worth. I don't care," Trump said. “I make – I have a lot of money, and far more than I ever thought I'd have. And I guess it's gone up. I don't even know.” Trump also said he has “a son who's a very straight, good guy. He watches over money. I don't even talk to him about it." Asked whether foreign investors in his companies, including World Liberty, believe they’re “buying influence” to get things they want from the U.S. government, Trump replied: "I don't know.” More: Trump faces criticism for seeking personal wealth through business deals while in office Other Democrats are planning to investigate Trump Trump’s 2025 financial disclosure declared he brought in $2.2 billion in 2025, with the bulk coming from $1.4 billion through the crypto industry . That includes more than $750 million from World Liberty Financial and $635 million in royalties and sales tied to his $TRUMP meme coin. Real estate assets and other holdings accounted for the rest of the president's 2025 income, which was more than three times the $622 million that his business ventures generated in 2024, according to The New York Times . Kushner, whose private equity firm Affinity Partners manages more than $6 billion, has drawn about 99% of that money from foreign sources, including $2 billion from Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund and funds linked to the governments of the United Arab Emirates and Qatar, according to an April letter from Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Maryland, the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee. Democrats say that’s especially concerning because Kushner has served as a key U.S. negotiator in the Middle East, including on Gaza and the war with Iran. Raskin, expected to chair the House Judiciary Committee, has said Democrats would subpoena the Trump family over its deals involving Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Qatar, including the "$400 million jet from Qatar" that Trump accepted. Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, the incoming chairman of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, sent records request letters two days after the election to World Liberty, Fight Fight Fight LLC – which runs the $TRUMP coin with a Trump Organization affiliate – and the crypto firms Binance and Tether. "Failure to voluntarily produce the requested records and information by January 4, 2027, will leave the Subcommittee with no choice but to consider alternative measures to obtain compliance," Blumenthal’s letters said. Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Oregon, expected to chair the Senate Finance Committee, posted one word on election night : "Subpoenas." In a statement outlining his agenda , Wyden said special interests that have "worked hand-in-hand with Trump" will "be forced to answer to the Senate Finance Committee for their role in hurting the American people and enabling Trump's corruption." Democrats acknowledge that Trump’s Justice Department is unlikely to enforce any consequences for those who don’t cooperate with their oversight efforts. But Democrats, Garcia said, will also “have the power of contempt charges. And contempt charges not only go to the DOJ, there's also a civil contempt process that goes to the courts.” This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Democrats are preparing to probe the Trump family's finances This article originally appeared on USA TODAY at https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2026/11/13/trump-made-billions-from-deals-now-dems-want-probes-and-answers/92694273007/

item.title: Report says Jensen Huang spent last hours as Nvidia CEO dejected: 'I don't care'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
(Bloomberg) -- At the end, Jensen Huang looked broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted. After weeks spent denying the allegations of infidelity and fighting to remain in his job as Nvidia Corp.’s chief executive officer, his surrender late Wednesday night was unconditional. Huang’s usual take-charge demeanor had evaporated, according to a person familiar with the situation, and he’d started using phrases like “whatever” and “I don’t care.” Most Read from Bloomberg Alice Huang, Suspected China Spy, Spent Years in Nvidia’s Orbit Nvidia Scandal Creates Risk for Entire AI Industry, Not Just CEO Alleged Chinese Spy at Heart of Nvidia Scandal Is in Beijing Mississippi Voters Pick Another Senator to Widen Democratic Win Elon Musk Says It Would Be an Honor to Hire Nvidia’s Huang For the decades he spent building Nvidia into a multitrillion-dollar AI chip behemoth, Huang was famous for his attention to the tiniest of details, from chip architecture to the compensation packages of even the most junior employees at the company. Now, in the eyes of the people in the room, he had given up. It was a stunningly quick fall for a billionaire and tech titan who two weeks ago was the face of artificial intelligence around the world. With his directness and vigor, he had charmed US President Donald Trump, shaped global tech policy and drawn adoring crowds on his papal-style international tours. It’s hard to imagine the current AI boom happening without Huang, his company and their chips, and it’s hard to imagine what it will look like after his fall. As Harvey Jones, chair of the company’s board of directors, wrote in an email to employees after Huang’s ouster, “Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world.” Huang couldn’t be reached for comment. When the news broke in late October that Huang had close ties with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, it looked like he would prevail. The board of directors, dominated by longtime investors, business partners and friends of Huang’s, was reluctant to act on the news stories, or even publicly comment on them. Most of the news coverage tiptoed around the exact nature of the CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang, the suspected spy. Huang denied to friends and colleagues that he had been unfaithful to his wife. He’d been denying it when questioned internally since late 2025. In one of his last interviews as CEO, Huang told Bloomberg News that his relationship with Alice Huang was typical of those with Chinese customers and executives. “It was all completely normal and not unusual,” he said. A turning point came last Friday, Nov. 6, when a Financial Times story cited US officials saying that the relationship had been a romantic one. Soon afterward, Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter went to Huang’s house to confront him, and Huang confessed. At that point, most of the board still didn’t want to take a public stance, but Teter, who is secretary of the board, told them they had to act. The next day, Saturday, the board announced that they would investigate the allegations. A prominent law firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, would lead the inquiry. On Sunday, Huang emailed the entire company, admitting to the affair, apologizing to his family and vowing to “cooperate fully” with the board’s investigation. As the scandal ballooned, there was evidence that it was, perhaps unsurprisingly, drawing Huang’s attention away from his extensive duties at the company. As part of Nvidia’s idiosyncratic org chart, Huang had around 60 executives at the company who reported to him, a small army by normal management standards. The whole company had to file emails with their top five priorities, which Huang used to check that everyone was working on what he considered most important. Normally he responded to them immediately at all hours of the day and night. In recent days the response times had grown longer. On Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Huang was also having an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care. This time, the board acted quickly. Directors assembled remotely on Wednesday, and the meeting lasted late into the night. In the end, Huang was given no choice but to resign, ending his association with the company completely. The next morning, the board announced Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress would step in as interim CEO. She was quick to try and reassure rattled employees. “I believe deeply in this company and in its future,” Kress wrote in an email reviewed by Bloomberg. “More than anything, I believe in each of you, in our customers and partners and in the vital role we play every day in the global economy. The Board, staff and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period and I want you to know how grateful we are for your resilience, professionalism and continued dedication. Thank you.” She pledged to hold an all-hands meeting on Nov. 18. The following day, Nvidia is due to report results and disclose what Wall Steet analysts predict will be a near doubling of quarterly sales growth. Now, the board confronts the difficult challenge of finding a replacement for Huang. Some executives considered likely to end up on the shortlist: Advanced Micro Devices Inc. CEO Lisa Su and Arm Holdings Plc CEO Rene Haas. It’s hard to imagine anyone filling all his roles — technologist, executive, marketer, lobbyist, mascot — and the company never bothered to create a traditional succession plan. For better or worse, Nvidia will begin to look more like a regular company going forward, managed in a more regular way. As for Huang himself, he won’t be able to retreat from public life, even if he wants to. In the coming weeks he’s expected to testify before Congress, where politicians will ask him about his relationship with Alice Huang and whether it might have put some of the secrets of Nvidia’s state-of-the-art chips at risk. According to people who’ve spoken with him in recent days, Huang has already taken a penitent turn, castigating himself as a “piece of sh--.” He claims not to care what happens to himself at this point. His main concern, he says, is his wife, and not “ruining the lives” of the multiple women now romantically linked to him in the public imagination. item.title: Bessent says Treasury favored limits on Megaspeed and places blame on Commerce
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Treasury Secretary Secretary Scott Bessent, picutred left alongside Secretary of State Marco Rubio, when Chinese President Xi Jinping visited the White House on September 24, 2026 (Brendan SMIALOWSKI) US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday blamed the Commerce Department for failing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore company at the center of a scandal that prompted Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang to resign. Speaking on CNBC, Bessent said Treasury, the Defense Department, the US Trade Representative's office and the State Department had backed adding Megaspeed to the Washington's trade blacklist, "for months." "But Commerce has the pen," Bessent said. "You will have to ask them about their internal processes." U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blames Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over Nvidia chip mess: "Treasury, War, USTR and State were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months." https://t.co/0BTlHymwUY — CNBC (@CNBC) November 13, 2026 He said he was "frustrated" because President Donald Trump "made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s." "Any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies, and in the AI race gives the Chinese an advantage," he said. The remarks are a rare public rebuke of one cabinet department by another. Commerce is led by Secretary Howard Lutnick. Megaspeed is suspected of helping Chinese firms get around US export controls by buying Nvidia chips for its data centers in Southeast Asia and routing them to China. The company reportedly traded more than $4 billion worth of Nvidia chips over two years. Its former director Alice Huang was this week identified in US media as an alleged Chinese intelligence asset who had a relationship with Jensen Huang. The two are not related. Beijing has denied the spying allegations. Jensen Huang acknowledged an extramarital affair in a November 8 letter to Nvidia employees that did not name the woman involved and resigned his position on Thursday. Nvidia's board has said it will investigate, and three US Congress committee chairs have asked him to attend a closed-door briefing on November 18. Bessent said coverage of the affair had focused too much on Huang's private life. "The story thus far has been on Jensen Huang's personal foibles," he said. "The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage." He questioned whether Nvidia had been selling to "what were obviously pass-through shell companies." "I think it's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that," Bessent said. He said there was "a lot of leakage in the system" and that the administration was "constantly working to close that down." arp/msp This article originally appeared on AFP at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/us-treasury-chief-blames-commerce-145607629.html

item.title: Users worldwide still facing Microsoft outage — but company says it sees progress
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Service across Microsoft's suite of services is slowly recovering from the massive global outage that began midday Thursday. Some users on the outage tracker Downdetector are reporting that Outlook email has started to return, but it appears the service isn't fully up and running for most users. In a status page update at 8 a.m. ET Friday, Microsoft reported that its recovery efforts were on track, “We're seeing continued recovery progress across affected regions, with broader improvements now observed in North America and sustained improvements across much of Europe,” the company said. “We're also seeing encouraging recovery signals in Asia Pacific, although some users may continue to experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery as mitigation progresses across the remaining affected infrastructure.” Outlook has more than an estimated 400 million active users worldwide. Teams is used by a reported 320 million people. The company said it had not yet found a fix for the issue, which affects multiple Microsoft 365 services that rely on Exchange Online, its email platform. In an update Friday at 7:09 a.m. ET, the company indicated it was making progress. "We're seeing encouraging recovery progress, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected Microsoft 365 infrastructure," Microsoft posted on X. "Some users may still experience intermittent issues as recovery actions continue." Microsoft did not provide a specific cause for the outage, but said the issue related to a number of servers being "unexpectedly unavailable." Microsoft executive vice president Charles Lamanna said on X there was "no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity." The Verge's Tom Warren reported that the outage may be related to a configuration issue with Microsoft Azure, its cloud computing platform. Government agencies in Japan, Singapore and Australia were among those affected, while the U.S. House of Representatives was also impacted by the outage. Politico reported one House staffer saying, "There goes a day of legislative work." AI companies OpenAI and Anthropic also reported facing issues. In the U.K, police and health services were impacted. In Taiwan, Reuters reported that one finance company started using fax machines to confirm trades. Australian home affairs minister Tony Burke said Microsoft had said it was dealing with something similar to the massive CrowdStrike outage in 2024. The problem began on Thursday, with Downdetector showing a major spike in outage reports, peaking just before 1 p.m. ET. Users reported problems with its Outlook, Copilot, Teams and Sharepoint services, and some even reported problems accessing Microsoft Word and Excel. In a message posted Thursday at 12:54 p.m. ET on the official Microsoft 365 Status account on X, the company said it was "investigating reports of users experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas." It subsequently confirmed that the issue may affect Microsoft 365 service connectivity for users "in any region." Just after 10 p.m. ET, Microsoft said its attempts to fix the issue were "not taking as expected." item.title: Alito warns Congress could 'turn off the lights' at Supreme Court
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito, speaking to the Federalist Society on Thursday, warned against any potential congressional action to defund the Supreme Court as he defended the importance of an independent judiciary. “Congress can turn off the lights at the Supreme Court and stop everything from happening if they want to defund their activities. And there are many, many, many other things that they can do, or at least try to do,” Alito said. “So, it is important to preserve the independence of the judiciary,” he added. “If that is eliminated, then the Constitution as adopted in 1789 will no longer be the same.” Alito made the comments in his return to the Federalist Society’s annual Antonin Scalia Memorial Dinner, named after the late conservative justice and held as part of the group’s annual convention each November. This year, the convention comes a week after Democrats swept control of both houses of Congress. Alito made no reference to the midterm elections or the pending change in power during his remarks, but Democrats have eyed using Congress's power of the purse as leverage against the conservative-majority court before. Two of Alito's colleagues — Justices Elena Kagan and Amy Coney Barrett — made a rare visit to Capitol Hill over the summer to advocate for increasing the judiciary's budget and increased security funding in the wake of rising threat levels. Alito told the crowd of more than 1,000 conservative lawyers on Thursday that the judiciary is the least powerful branch and it is “vulnerable” to Congress and the executive. Still, the justice warned that judges can overstep. “If you think about a hand grenade, a 500-pound bomb and a nuclear weapon,” he began, “the hand grenade is the least dangerous. But that is not to say that it is not dangerous.” The justice chastised lower judges at one point for sometimes issuing “unjustified” orders blocking presidents’ policies in recent years. “They are dedicated and they are skillful, but they’re not perfect and they make mistakes,” Alito said. “And in some instances, I think they have gone far astray in abuse of their powers.” Alito was the latest conservative justice to address the Federalist Society’s annual dinner. Justice Brett Kavanaugh and Barrett shared the stage last year, and Justice Neil Gorsuch joined former Justice Stephen Breyer a year prior . Alito addressed the dinner virtually during the pandemic in a speech where he described the health crisis as having caused “previously unimaginable” restrictions on civil liberties. The Federalist Society does not officially take political or legal positions, but the nonprofit over decades has become an incubator for Republican judicial nominees and a tentpole of the conservative legal movement. item.title: Van Hollen takes on Schumer for majority leader after Democrats flip Senate
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said Thursday that he will run for Senate Majority Leader in the next Congress, setting up a challenge to Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer after the party swept to power in the midterm elections. Van Hollen said in a statement that “the American people called for change” and that is why he is running. “It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership,” Van Hollen said. “This is not about any one person — it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.” Schumer has said he has the necessary support to win the race, which will be the first contested election for Senate Democratic leader in decades. The closed-door, secret-ballot election will be held in early December. The question of whether to reelect Schumer has already divided the caucus and many senators have declined to say publicly how they will vote, even before Van Hollen entered the race. They have privately deliberated about what message to take from the election and many are torn — Schumer recruited many of the party’s winning candidates and raised money for them, but progressive groups are pushing for his removal. Making the pitch for his reelection, Schumer has been working with Democratic senators one-on-one to form an agenda for 2027. In private caucus meetings this week, Schumer opened discussion on a broad plan for their first 100 days in power that included healthcare and tariff legislation and efforts to stop the Iran war. “I’m going to win it,” Schumer told The Associated Press in an interview last week. In a statement after Van Hollen’s announcement, Schumer said he welcomes any discussion about the future of the caucus. “I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader,” Schumer said. “I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people.” Divisions over Schumer have simmered over the last two years While Schumer is the favorite to win, Van Hollen’s run exposes a rift in the party that opened in the spring of 2025 , when Schumer was put on the defensive after he sided with Republicans on a spending vote. Even as Schumer has redeemed himself within his caucus since then — leading them through a government shutdown last year and orchestrating huge wins in the election — many in the Democratic base are agitating for generational change. Van Hollen, 67, is not that much younger than Schumer, 75. But he has positioned himself as a new face in the party. He has also said he is considering a run for president. While most Democratic senators have either said they are supporting Schumer or are undecided, Van Hollen has at least two backers: Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, who won a competitive election in his state last week, and progressive standard-bearer Bernie Sanders . El-Sayed posted on X Thursday night that their majority will need “bold leadership.” “I called on Sen. @ChrisVanHollen to lead our caucus as a candidate back in April because he leads with courage and experience,” El-Sayed wrote. “We need both right now. Which is why I’m proud to stand with him in his bid to lead our Senate majority.” Sen. Sanders, an independent who caucuses with the Democrats, held a press conference Tuesday announcing he would not support Schumer. He posted Thursday night that the American people “want a Democratic Party that will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families. That is why I am supporting Senator Chris Van Hollen to lead Senate Democrats.” Van Hollen has not yet laid out his own agenda, but he has criticized Schumer for his ties to Israel and other special interests. While Schumer has a long history of support for Israel, he has strongly criticized Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his handling of the war in Gaza. Schumer says he has broad support Several senators have said they are backing Schumer, including incoming Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown , who beat Republican Sen. Jon Husted last week. Beyond the election wins, those who support him say being the leader is a difficult job, experience is necessary and Schumer has proven himself with legislative successes when they held the Senate under President Joe Biden. “Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?” posted Maine Sen. Angus King, another independent who caucuses with Democrats and votes in the leadership election. “Chuck Schumer is one of the principal architects of the most successful election in modern history, and I see no reason to change the leadership that helped make that success possible,” King wrote. Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto, D-Nev., also posted her support Thursday evening: Cortez Masto said Schumer was key in “securing a historic majority. I will be supporting him as our Democratic leader.” This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/sen-chris-van-hollen-maryland-020344480.html

item.title: D.C. shooting suspect was suing his condo association. Man killed was the building manager.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON – As police investigate why a board-certified emergency physician might have opened fire in a Washington, DC, neighborhood Nov. 12, they pointed to a lawsuit against his homeowners association as potentially playing a role. Police said Matt Wade Lambert, a 55-year-old healthcare professional, shot and killed his building manager, James Stuart, in a DC gym before barricading himself inside his apartment and shooting four additional people from his patio early in the morning on Nov. 12. Lambert also shot and killed himself, police said. One of the shooting victims remains in critical condition, while the other three do not have life threatening injuries, police said. Those who knew Lambert said they were shocked. His professional acquaintances described Lambert as a “genuine” and “good” person in conversations with USA TODAY. His attorney, Joel Braithwaite, said during a news conference that life appeared to be looking up for Lambert before the shooting, noting that he was scheduled to begin a new job Nov. 16. Braithwaite said Lambert gave no indication that he was at a breaking point during a phone conversation they had Nov. 10. Lambert, who worked as a consultant for healthcare administrators, had spoken at a conference in Orlando, earlier in the week. Craig Hauben, a fellow panelist at the event and the CEO of the software development firm Clutch, said Lambert seemed “jovial” at the time. He did not mention anything about ongoing litigation with his building, Hauben said. Court documents reveal Lambert has been enmeshed in litigation with his condo association since 2025 over water damage and black mold in his unit that he said stemmed from construction to the building. Lambert’s dispute with Metropole Condominium Association Back in March 2023, the HOA began work on the condo's façade to remediate the building envelope, according to a court filing by Lambert against the Metropole Condominium Association on March 21, 2025. Between May 2023 and April 2024, Lambert paid the association’s special assessment for the building envelope remediation that totaled $15,356.95, according to court documents. During the construction, Lambert said his “unit experienced suspected water intrusion, mold, significant moisture accumulation, and/or related damage,” according to the March 21, 2025 court filing. Lambert said he communicated to the association that there were instances of water intrusion in his unit in March 2024. A hole was cut into the drywall in Lambert’s residence in August 2024 to investigate whether water was running behind the wall, according to court filings. By September 2024, Lambert alleged in court documents that there was excess moisture being collected behind the drywall and his electrical curtains had stopped working. He also said that same month that mold was visible and detectable by smell, according to the court filings. He retained mold remediation expert ServPro on Sept. 20, 2024 to conduct an assessment of suspected mold that was visible from the hole that building officials cut above his windows back in August 2024. The inspection said: “Visible mold contamination was observed on exterior and interior walls, due to possible water intrusion,” according to an excerpt included in the filings. Lambert on Oct. 9, 2024 asked the Metropole Condominium Association to take action against the mold and excess moisture based on the independent inspections, as well as provide reimbursement for the costs of the assessments. Lambert said in court documents that he incurred expenses in excess of $82,000 "as a result of Defendant’s inaction to remedy any of the effect of its building envelope repair on Unit 704." Later in October 2024, Lambert and the condo association traded letters over the repairs that Lambert was going to do and whether he would be refunded by the group. The back-and-forth between Lambert and the condo association spiraled into a more than yearlong legal battle that included Stuart, the building manager, as a witness, as well as VIDA Fitness as a defendant. According to court documents, VIDA, located on the ground floor of the condo building, would use commercial dryers that Lambert alleged would “discharge warm, moist air that is vented up through a mechanical shaft to a dryer vent fan on the roof.” An engineering consulting firm hired by another plaintiff found that the elevated moisture levels in Lambert’s apartment were likely caused by the dryers, according to the court filing. USA TODAY could not immediately reach the attorneys for the condo association or VIDA Fitness. Braithwaite said he does not know what might have triggered Lambert ahead of the shooting. He noted it was the anniversary of when Lambert buried his mother. “I don't think there's any sense to be made,” Braithwaite said. “There's nothing that I can say from my mind that brings any closure to it.” This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: What court documents reveal about DC shooting suspect's HOA issues This article originally appeared on USA TODAY at https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/crime/2026/11/12/dc-shooting-what-we-know/92746956007/

item.title: Deadly building collapse brought Brooklyn neighbors together. Now they want answers.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Emergency personnel work at the scene of a partial building collapse where, according to local reports, people are trapped in the Brooklyn borough of New York, on Wednesday, November 11. - Angelina Katsanis/Reuters Leonor Yupa dropped to her knees Thursday when a Spanish-language media reporter said her 22-year-old son was among eight people whose lives were claimed by the Brooklyn building collapse the day before. “I want my son! I want my son!” the Ecuadorian mother cried in Spanish as family members tried to hold Yupa up and others who gathered at Bethesda Church of God in Christ assured her the reports were unconfirmed. The agonizing cries of another woman who just lost her husband reverberated through the Brooklyn sanctuary across the street from the collapse. When the woman learned her husband’s body was pulled from the debris Thursday morning, she collapsed and wailed her husband’s name. “Tomás! Tomasito!” she cried. Family members gathered around the widow and formed a prayer circle. Just outside the church, a nervous father also prayed. He was anxiously waiting to learn the fate of his son, a construction worker who has not been reachable since the collapse. In the Flatbush neighborhood – home to a mix of immigrant communities – six adults and two children had died and over a dozen were injured after the three-story mixed-use building collapsed on Veterans Day, a day on which many families stayed home. unknown content item - “I want to take a moment to remember those we have so senselessly lost,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani told reporters Thursday. “These were our friends and our neighbors, parents and children, young families building their lives in our city, and immigrants from Mexico, Colombia, Ecuador, Trinidad, and beyond.” The day after the tragedy, residents and other bystanders crowded the sidewalk as construction equipment was used to removed debris and rubble from the site. Clothes still hung from a closet in an adjoining building where a wall came down during the collapse. A construction worker embraces a child at the scene of the collapse on Wednesday. - Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images North America/Getty Images A heavy rain pelted the intersection of Flatbush and Bedford avenues, a multicultural enclave that is the heart of New York City’s Caribbean diaspora. The names on signs of storefront churches and businesses – from bakeries, restaurants and beauty salons – reflect places like Jamaica, Haiti, Trinidad and Tobago, and more recently, newcomers from Mexico and Ecuador. Among those killed Wednesday were three Colombian citizens, two Ecuadorian men and a 26-year-old Guatemalan man, officials from the countries announced. In the aftermath of the collapse, local families, clergy and community groups gathered to support one another while demanding accountability for housing conditions and construction oversight in their predominantly Black and immigrant neighborhood. ‘Go in the church and pray, please’ On Wednesday night, Yupa and other relatives spent hours scouring hospitals throughout Brooklyn hoping to find her son, Gabriel Siguencia. The family then visited the collapse site Thursday. Yupa shielded herself from heavy rain under the canopy of the church as a woman with a West Indian lilt alerted other bystanders nearby that she saw first responders pull a young child and a woman from the rubble. Then came the news about Siguencia, who had arrived in New York from Ecuador only about a month ago and started working as a carpenter at the construction site adjacent to the building collapse about two weeks ago, according to uncles, cousins and family friends. “He came to America looking for the same opportunities that people from all over the world come here for,” said family friend Javier Ortega, who drove Siguencia’s mother to the site from her home in Connecticut. “That’s why he was working there.” Like many other families, Siguencia’s loved ones awaited news about him across the street from the collapse site. Some, like the husband of a six-month pregnant woman rescued from the rubble, rejoiced as they received word their loved one was safe. unknown content item - As the downpour intensified Thursday over the neighborhood known as “Little Haiti,” a member of Bethesda Church of God in Christ invited Siguencia’s family inside the warm vestibule. Yupa, weeping, sat on a folding chair as a Haitian church member served her cups of water. As Yupa sobbed, family members surrounded her and Ecuadoran consular officials made calls trying to track down information. Soft murmurs of “Hallelujah, hallelujah” spilled out from the church filled with Haitian worshippers on the other side of the vestibule doors. “We all have to look out for each other in this country,” said the woman who brought water to Yupa and the others. “It doesn’t matter where you come from.” Another woman implored Yupa as she wept: “Go in the church and pray, please.” Time ticked by with a heaviness before officials with the Ecuadoran consul walked Yupa and her friends and family members several blocks in the heavy rain to a nearby YMCA, where relatives of the dead and missing had been gathering. The consul general of Ecuador, Gicela Andrade Valens, later told reporters outside that authorities had confirmed Siguencia’s death to his mother. Another Ecuadorian national, 26-year-old José Luis Caguana Cosquillo, was also killed. “We express our deepest condolences to his family and loved ones, and we stand with them in profound solidarity in these moments of grief,” the consulate said. Colombia’s consulate in New York said two Colombian children and one adult were killed in the collapse. “The Consulate of Colombia in New York reiterates its most sincere condolences to the victims’ families and loved ones,” the consulate said. ‘Nothing like this has ever happened in this neighborhood’ Pastor Alfred Justin Joseph’s church, the Bethesda Church of God in Christ, became an open sanctuary for the injured, the anxious and the grieving. “They were standing in the street. I let them in,” Joseph said. “Thank God we have counselors in the church — people who do counseling for grief.” Various groups have streamed through his church, including a dozen people in the first wave. While some have since been escorted to a local YMCA or hotels, the church remains an epicenter of consolation and support. As she heard the wailing of the young woman who lost her spouse in the collapse, Flatbush resident Joy Kerr led a prayer circle to offer some comfort in a moment of devastation. Kerr walked into the church and found the young woman crying hysterically after learning that her spouse, a construction worker, was killed when the building came down. Kerr listened to the woman sobbing for about half an hour and said, “No, I can’t take this. I can’t sit back and just watch her and listen to her cry so hysterically.” “In that moment, I knew she needed comfort,” she said. She gathered with the woman who had lost her spouse and those around them, and they began to pray. “This is devastating,” Kerr said. “Nothing like this has ever happened in this neighborhood, and we just need to come together and stay together as a community.” unknown content item - And Katie Stevens, a teacher who lives about a block from the building, sobbed after she watched first responders load body bags into a van Thursday morning. “I care for my neighbors so much,” Stevens told CNN. “I’m just so sad.” James Williams, a bricklayer who has lived in the neighborhood for 35 years, stood across the street from the wreckage site Thursday and recalled watching the building’s walls cave in the day before. One image reverberated in his mind: a woman climbing a now-exposed staircase as everything around her was crumbling. “I don’t know if she got out alive or not,” he lamented. “To see that and not know what happened to her…I might have to go see a psychiatrist.” Williams said he knows multiple families affected by the collapse. A friend told him she had been texting with relatives at the site when it collapsed but had not been able to locate them at any local hospitals. As grief rippled through the neighborhood, nonprofits and agencies including the Red Cross, NYC Human Resources Administration and World Central Kitchen helped shaken families with emergency shelter, supplies and updates about missing people. Neighbors call for accountability Officials stand at the site on Thursday - Yuki Iwamura/AP As darkness fell over the collapse site Thursday night, amid thunderclaps and heavy rain, floodlights shone on a now-idle backhoe that had been excavating piles of debris, twisted metal and the pieces of what had been apartments into dumpsters. Crews finished a marathon search through the rubble and determined there were no more survivors to be rescued, officials had said Thursday afternoon. Under umbrellas, people hurried home after work, some stopping momentarily to look at the now-vacant space that had recently been home to many. Across the street, a cluster of older women started gathering early for an evening service at Bethesda Church of God in Christ. “This church happens to be a Haitian Creole speaking church, but the church is open to the entire community,” said Florence Saint-Jean, a psychologist who offers mental health and trauma services at the church. “The people who live here are immigrants, and so when crisis happens, there’s only one language – love,” she said. “People are tired, they’re looking for food, they’re looking for shelter, and the church is always open and available.” As neighbors hugged and comforted one another, one question created knots in their chests: How could this tragedy have happened? The Department of Buildings has not yet determined the cause of the collapse, and an investigation is underway as new information emerges about the building’s history and construction process. New York officials are looking into what caused the collapse of the building built in 1930, with Mamdani vowing to hold anyone responsible “fully accountable” and authorities inspecting about 100 locations throughout the city linked to the site. The Brooklyn District Attorney’s Office is conducting its own investigation into whether laws were broken. “We are working closely with the Department of Buildings and our law enforcement partners to determine whether any criminal conduct contributed to this tragedy,” district attorney Eric Gonzalez said in a statement Thursday. As investigators try to determine factors in Wednesday’s deadly collapse of the three-story building in Brooklyn, they’ll be looking at both the condition of the collapsed building and activity at the construction site that neighbored it. Cracks had been reported in the facade of the building as part of the permitting process for construction on the adjacent lot, which the collapse spilled into. The building’s owner, Olufemi Falade , has a troubling history that reportedly landed him in jail for 12 days in 2006 for failing to repair hundreds of violations across multiple buildings. The collapsed building at 1321 Flatbush Avenue currently has 98 open housing violations – ranging from unsafe electrical wiring and a lack of smoke detectors to bedbug infestations and a lack of adequate water supply for the building’s sprinkler system – according to records from the New York City Department of Housing Preservation and Development. CNN has reached out to Falade for comment. Though building collapses are rare in the US, lower-income and immigrant neighborhoods often face higher risks of hazards and neglect. Housing experts and advocates have pointed to systemic inequities that disproportionately impact working class immigrant communities, including old buildings, lax code enforcement and rapid construction. Sumathy Kumar, executive director of New York State Tenant Bloc and Housing Justice for All, an organization that works to organize tenants, said the Brooklyn landlord has an extensive and troubling history with the city. “We need better and faster tools to hold landlords accountable and to make sure that buildings are properly maintained and managed,” Kumar said. Saint-Jean said there is a visible distinction between how development occurs in immigrant communities like Flatbush. “What we’re most concerned about is, when things like his happen, that our voice (is) not being heard about development in the area,” she said. CNN’s Ray Sanchez reported from New York and Dalia Faheid from Los Angeles.
